kurals.tamil:
குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம் மடியென்னும்
மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudiyennum kundraa vilakkam madiyennum
Maasoora maaindhu kedum.
kurals.meaning: A family is like a lamp whose light should never fail, but when the grime of laziness settles on it, its light fades and goes out.
kurals.elementary: Think of a lamp that has shone in your home for years. If nobody cleans the soot off the glass, the light gets dimmer and dimmer until the room is dark. Laziness is that soot: a family stays bright only if its people keep working and caring.
kurals.university: The opening couplet sets up the chapter’s governing image: குடி (family, lineage) is a குன்றா விளக்கம், a lamp or radiance that of itself would never diminish, and மடி (sloth) is the மாசு, the grime or darkness that ‘spreads over’ (ஊர) it until it dims (மாய்ந்து) and perishes (கெடும்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read மாசு as a film of dirt that accumulates by degrees, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and the Rev. Drew/Pope tradition render it as darkness; either way the point is that decline is gradual and self-inflicted rather than sudden and external. The chapter heading மடியின்மை (‘absence of sloth’) follows ஊக்கமுடைமை (ch. 60, energy) and precedes ஆள்வினையுடைமை (ch. 62, manly effort), so Valluvar moves from the positive virtue to the vice that undoes it before turning to sustained effort. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org; the latter prints the older sandhi-joined form (விளக்க மடியென்னு / மாசூர) with no change of wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Arjun, tamo guṇa, which is born of ignorance, is the cause of illusion for the embodied souls. It deludes all living beings through negligence, laziness, and sleep.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names tamas, literally ‘darkness’, as the quality that binds people through negligence (pramāda), laziness (ālasya) and sleep (nidrā).
hinduism.tie_back: Tamas as a darkness born of laziness is almost exactly the Kural’s image of sloth as the grime that dims the family lamp.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on laziness as darkness; the Gita speaks of the individual soul, not the family line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept. … And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the ten virgins, the careless ones let their lamps go out and are shut out of the wedding feast.
christianity.tie_back: A lamp that goes out through neglect is the same picture as the Kural’s family light dying under sloth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close image match; the parable’s fault is unpreparedness for the Kingdom rather than household sloth as such.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah! I seek refuge with you (Allah) from (worries) care and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from being heavily in debt and from being overpowered by other men.”
islam.explanation: Anas reports that the Prophet prayed this often, listing laziness (kasal) among the things a believer should seek God’s protection from.
islam.tie_back: Treating laziness as a danger to be warded off matches the Kural’s view of sloth as the stain that ruins a household.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear condemnation of laziness; the hadith has no lamp image and does not mention the family line.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Through slothfulness the ceiling sags, / Through lazy hands the house caves in.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet notes that a house does not collapse all at once; it sags and leaks gradually when its owners are idle.
judaism.tie_back: The slowly failing house is the Hebrew counterpart of the Kural’s slowly dimming family lamp.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 10:18 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: gradual ruin of a ‘house’ through sloth; the Hebrew bayit also carries the sense of household.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Saṅgārava Sutta, the Buddha compares a mind overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) to a bowl of water covered with moss and water plants, in which a man cannot see the reflection of his own face.
buddhism.explanation: Sloth and torpor is one of the five hindrances; like a film over water, it hides what should be clearly seen, including one’s own good.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s மாசு (grime) spreading over a lamp and the Buddha’s moss spreading over clear water are the same image of sloth as a covering film.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good image parallel; the sutta concerns mental clarity rather than family fortune.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the start of the Odyssey, the house of Odysseus is being eaten up by the suitors while young Telemachus sits passive, until Athena, disguised as Mentes, rouses him to act for his father’s house.
greek_mythology.explanation: The great house is wasting away not because of an outside attack but because its heir has not yet stirred himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s dimming lamp, a noble house fades while its heir stays inactive and revives only when he rouses himself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Telemachus is young and unsure rather than lazy, so this is an analogy of situation, not of vice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Way to Wealth, Benjamin Franklin’s Poor Richard warns that sloth, like rust, eats away faster than work wears things out, while a key that is used stays bright.
philosophy.explanation: Franklin argues that idleness wears things away more than work does, and that constant use keeps things bright.
philosophy.tie_back: Franklin’s rust on an unused key and the Kural’s grime on a neglected lamp are the same image of sloth tarnishing what should shine.
philosophy.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong image parallel (tarnish versus brightness); paraphrased because the wording was not re-verified against a live text.

kurals.tamil:
மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல் குடியைக்
குடியாக வேண்டு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Madiyai madiyaa ozhugal kudiyaik
Kudiyaaga vendu bavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who want their family to be a family in the full, honoured sense must see laziness for the ruin it is and put it to death in how they live.
kurals.elementary: If you want your team to be a real team, you can’t treat ‘I’ll do it later’ as harmless. You have to see laziness as the thing that breaks teams, and push it out every day. Families work the same way.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a double pun. மடியை மடியா can mean ‘treating sloth as sloth’, recognising it for the vice it is (Varadarasanar: சோம்பலைச் சோம்பலாகக் கொண்டு), or, because மடி also means ‘to die, perish’, ‘treating sloth as something to be killed’ or ‘as death itself’. Kalaignar’s gloss (சோம்பலை ஒழித்து) takes the second sense. The echo குடியைக் குடியாக, ‘to make the family a family’, implies that a lineage only truly exists as a குடி while it keeps its standing; Parimelazhagar takes குடி here as the illustrious family, not the bare kin-group. ஒழுகல், ‘conduct, practice’, makes this a matter of daily habit, not of a single resolution. Both source texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined மடியா வொழுகல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa’s ‘charaiveti’ (keep moving) verses, Indra tells Rohita that fortune sits still with the one who sits and sleeps with the one who sleeps, and each stanza ends with the refrain: keep moving on.
hinduism.explanation: The god Indra urges the prince Rohita to keep wandering and striving, teaching that stillness and sleep bring decline while effort brings prosperity.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells a prince who wants his line to prosper to reject sloth completely and keep acting.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Thematically close and also addressed to a royal heir; paraphrased because the verse numbering and wording vary between editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists freedom from sloth, together with fervour of spirit, among the marks of a life given over to God.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like Valluvar, makes rejecting sloth a daily rule of conduct (ஒழுகல்), not an occasional effort.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear rejection of sloth; Paul addresses the church community rather than a family line.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says the strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak one, and tells believers to strive for what benefits them, seek God’s help, and not give way to helplessness.
islam.explanation: The hadith tells believers to strive energetically for what is beneficial and forbids giving in to incapacity or listlessness (ʿajz).
islam.tie_back: Refusing to ‘give up’ matches the Kural’s demand that anyone who wants to raise their family must put sloth to death.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased (the live text could not be re-fetched); strong on striving but says nothing about family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Tarfon said: the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the laborers are indolent, and the reward is great, and the master of the house is insistent.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon describes the human condition as a short working day with much to do, and names laziness as the workers’ typical failing.
judaism.tie_back: Tarfon’s ‘indolent labourers’ are the people Valluvar warns: a house (bayit / குடி) is only upheld when that laziness is overcome.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:15 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the danger of indolence; the ‘house’ here is God’s, not the worker’s family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, the Buddha’s last words to his monks are that all conditioned things are subject to decay, and they should strive on with diligence (appamādena sampādetha).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s final teaching makes diligence, the opposite of heedless sloth, the one thing his followers must hold on to.
buddhism.tie_back: Just as the Kural makes killing sloth the condition for a family’s survival, the Buddha makes diligence the condition for the community’s survival after him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the context is spiritual liberation, not household standing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that a household’s stores are filled only by those who refuse to procrastinate.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s full barn, like the Kural’s thriving குடி, belongs only to the one who treats sloth as the enemy.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 410-412 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit and also about household prosperity; Hesiod focuses on procrastination specifically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If, therefore, you will be negligent and slothful, and always add procrastination to procrastination, purpose to purpose, and fix day after day in which you will attend to yourself, you will insensibly continue without proficiency”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that someone who keeps putting off self-reform because of sloth will slide, without noticing, into a life of no progress.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus, like Valluvar, says that sloth has to be named and stopped now, not managed later.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 50 in Carter’s numbering (51 in some editions)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the vice; Epictetus is concerned with the individual’s moral progress rather than a lineage.

kurals.tamil:
மடிமடிக் கொண்டொழுகும் பேதை பிறந்த
குடிமடியும் தன்னினும் முந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Madimadik kondozhugum pedhai pirandha
Kudimadiyum thanninum mundhu.
kurals.meaning: When a fool clings to destructive laziness, the family he was born into dies even before he does.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a boy who never helps and never learns, and lets his family’s shop fall apart. The sad part is that the shop can close long before he grows old. His laziness hurts his family first.
kurals.university: Valluvar makes மடி ring three times: மடி (sloth) … மடி … மடியும் (perishes). The phrase மடிமடிக் கொண்டு is read in two ways. Varadarasanar and Parimelazhagar take the second மடி as an adjective, ‘sloth that destroys’ (அழிக்கும் இயல்புடைய சோம்பல்). Others hear மடி in its everyday sense of ‘lap’, ‘holding sloth in his lap’, cherishing it; Pappaiah’s ‘the sloth that ought to be cast off’ is close to this. பேதை, ‘fool’, is a strong word in the Kural (see ch. 84, பேதைமை): the fault is presented as a failure of understanding, not just of energy. The paradox that the குடி dies ‘before himself’ (தன்னினும் முந்து) means that the family’s standing, its reputation and wealth, can die while its lazy member is still alive to see it. Both source texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms குடிமடியுந் தன்னினு முந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which covers the nature of the self from beginning to end, and which is derived from sleep, indolence, and negligence, is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies the pleasure people get from sleep, laziness and carelessness as tamasic: it deludes a person from start to finish.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘fool’ (பேதை) who holds on to sloth is exactly the person deluded by tamasic pleasure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on sloth as delusion; the Gita does not say the family perishes first.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.”
christianity.explanation: Paul sets out a blunt rule for the Thessalonian community: whoever refuses to work has no claim on others’ support.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like Valluvar, treats the person who clings to idleness as someone who has cut himself off from the life of the household that feeds him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the condemnation of chosen idleness, but has nothing like the Kural’s claim that the family dies before the idler.

islam.quote_or_event: “There are two blessings that many people are deceived into losing: health and free time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that people commonly squander health and leisure, not realising what they have until it is gone.
islam.tie_back: The deceived squanderer of free time is the Kural’s பேதை, who wastes his chances until his family’s fortune is gone.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures the foolish waste of opportunity; says nothing about family decline.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, / By the vineyard of someone lacking sense. / It was all overgrown with thorns; / Its surface was covered with chickweed, / And its stone fence lay in ruins.”
judaism.explanation: The sage describes the estate of a lazy man ‘lacking sense’, now overgrown and with its walls fallen, as a lesson in how sloth ruins what was inherited.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Lazy’ and ‘lacking sense’ appear together here, as in the Kural’s மடி and பேதை, and the ruined estate stands for the family that dies before its owner.
judaism.source: Proverbs 24:30-31 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: the lazy fool’s patrimony is ruined while he still lives.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a man who has youth and strength but wastes them in sloth and idle thinking, and so never reaches wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts pair sloth with folly: the idler never finds wisdom, and the Kural’s பேதை loses his family.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on sloth as folly; the loss here is wisdom, not family.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the Ant and the Grasshopper, the grasshopper sings away the summer while the ant stores grain, and when winter comes the grasshopper starves.
greek_mythology.explanation: The idler enjoys the present and ignores the season for work, then finds himself with nothing when need arrives.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s fool, the grasshopper pays for his idleness before he expects to.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Ants and the Grasshopper (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A Greek fable rather than myth; it shows ruin through sloth but has no family or lineage theme.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book VIII of the Republic, Socrates describes the idle spendthrift as a ‘drone’ in a household, a plague to the house just as a drone is to the hive, who uses up its wealth while contributing nothing.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the drone to picture the member of a family or city who consumes without working and so brings ruin on the whole.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s drone that ruins the house matches the Kural’s idle fool whose family perishes before he does.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close image; Plato’s main concern is the oligarchic city rather than a single lineage.

kurals.tamil:
குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும் மடிமடிந்து
மாண்ட உஞற்றி லவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudimadindhu kutram perugum madimadindhu
Maanda unjatri lavarkku.
kurals.meaning: For those who sink into laziness and make no worthy effort, the family’s standing collapses and their faults keep multiplying.
kurals.elementary: When you stop doing your homework, it’s not just one problem. Soon you’re behind, you start making excuses, and you get into more trouble. Laziness is like a door that lets many other problems in, and the whole family feels it.
kurals.university: The couplet names two consequences: குடி மடிந்து, ‘the family perishing’, and குற்றம் பெருகும், ‘faults multiplying’. It gives one cause: மடி மடிந்து, ‘having fallen into sloth’. Here மடிந்து is used in the sense of ‘sinking’ or ‘being caught’, which Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss as சோம்பலில் அகப்பட்டு / வீழ்வதால். The rare word உஞற்று (effort, exertion) together with மாண்ட (excellent, worthy) specifies what is missing: not activity of any kind but dignified, purposeful effort (Pope’s ‘noble objects’). Parimelazhagar notes that idleness is productive, of vice, which fits a line of Indian moral thought in which inactivity invites other faults. The same second-line phrase recurs in 607 (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), which ties the two couplets together. Both sources agree; the older text has the sandhi forms பெருகு மடிமடிந்து and மாண்ட வுஞற்றி.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You should thus perform your prescribed Vedic duties, since action is superior to inaction. By ceasing activity, even your bodily maintenance will not be possible.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna argues that action is better than inaction: even keeping the body alive requires work, so giving up activity leads to decline.
hinduism.tie_back: If idleness cannot sustain even one body, it certainly cannot sustain a family, which is the Kural’s குடி மடிந்து.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Supports the decline side of the Kural; does not address the multiplying of faults.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul observes that idleness does not stay alone: it soon turns into gossip, meddling and improper speech.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies’ is a precise illustration of குற்றம் பெருகும், faults multiplying from sloth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on sloth multiplying faults; the context is a specific group in the early church.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the hypocrites [think to] deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. And when they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing [themselves to] the people and not remembering Allah except a little,”
islam.explanation: The Quran links laziness in worship with a cluster of further faults: hypocrisy, showing off, and neglect of the remembrance of God.
islam.tie_back: Laziness appearing alongside several other vices mirrors the Kural’s claim that faults multiply around sloth.
islam._accuracy_note: Laziness here is a symptom of hypocrisy rather than its cause, so the parallel is partial.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer says: Even if she brought him a hundred maidservants, he can compel her to make thread from wool, since idleness leads to licentiousness. … Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: … since idleness leads to idiocy.”
judaism.explanation: In a ruling about household duties, two sages state a general principle: idleness breeds immorality and dulls the mind, so no one in a household should be entirely without work.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Idleness leads to’ further faults is the rabbinic form of the Kural’s குற்றம் பெருகும், and it is also set in the context of the household.
judaism.source: Mishnah Ketubot 5:5 (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong principle match; the specific ruling on wives’ work reflects its own era.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man who is fond of sleep and company, inactive and lazy, and manifesting anger —this is the cause of his downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Discourse on Downfall, the Buddha lists sleepiness, idleness and laziness, together with anger, as the third cause of a person’s ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Laziness appearing next to other faults and leading to downfall parallels both halves of the Kural: faults multiply, and the house declines.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipāta 1.6, Parābhava Sutta (trans. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on sloth with other faults leading to decline; ‘downfall’ is personal rather than explicitly familial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Both gods and men are angry with a man who lives idle, for in nature he is like the stingless drones who waste the labour of the bees, eating without working”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod calls the idle man a drone who eats what others have worked for, and says he earns the anger of gods and men alike.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The drone’s idleness brings both waste and disgrace, which is the Kural’s double outcome of a ruined family and growing fault.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 302-306 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on idleness as wasteful and blameworthy; does not describe faults multiplying as such.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay ‘Of Idleness’, Montaigne compares an idle mind to fallow land that, left alone, grows a mass of wild and useless weeds, and says it produces fantastic ‘chimeras’ unless kept busy with a fixed purpose.
philosophy.explanation: Montaigne observes from his own retirement that an unoccupied mind does not rest but runs wild and breeds disorder.
philosophy.tie_back: Montaigne’s weed-choked field of the mind is a vivid picture of the Kural’s faults multiplying in the absence of worthy effort.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays I.8, ‘Of Idleness’ (trans. C. Cotton)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; Montaigne describes mental disorder rather than family decline.

kurals.tamil:
நெடுநீர் மறவி மடிதுயில் நான்கும்
கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Neduneer maravi madidhuyil naangum
Keduneeraar kaamak kalan.
kurals.meaning: Procrastination, forgetfulness, laziness and oversleeping are the four things people bound for ruin love to board, like a pleasure boat carrying them to disaster.
kurals.elementary: Imagine four friends who always say: ‘Do it later’, ‘Oops, I forgot’, ‘I’m too tired’, and ‘Just five more minutes of sleep.’ They feel comfy, like a boat ride, but the boat is floating toward a waterfall. Good habits are how you steer the boat back.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s best-known couplet and its most careful analysis. It lists four linked dispositions: நெடுநீர், literally ‘long-drawn nature’, i.e. procrastination (Varadarasanar: காலம் நீட்டித்தல்); மறவி, forgetfulness or heedlessness (compare ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை); மடி, sloth; and துயில், excessive sleep. It calls them the காமக் கலன் of the கெடுநீரார், ‘those whose nature is to perish’. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators take கலன் as a vessel or ship (மரக்கலம்; Pappaiah: சிறு படகு), giving Pope’s ‘pleasure-boat … to ruin’s shore’. Because கலன் can also mean ‘ornament’, some readers take the line as ‘the ornaments the doomed love to wear’, but the vessel reading is standard. The rhyme நெடுநீர் / கெடுநீரார் binds cause to result. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss of நெடுநீர் as ‘long weeping’ is idiosyncratic and not followed by the classical commentators. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (மடிதுயி னான்குங்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The six faults should be avoided by a person who wisheth to attain prosperity, viz., sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, indolence and procrastination.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura advises King Dhritarashtra that anyone who wants prosperity must give up six faults, which include sleep, indolence and procrastination.
hinduism.tie_back: Three of Vidura’s six (sleep, indolence, procrastination) are three of Valluvar’s four, and both are warnings addressed to rulers about ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva 33 (Vidura Nīti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one catalogue of the same vices; Vidura adds fear and anger and does not use the boat image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation.”
christianity.explanation: In Gethsemane, the disciples fall asleep at the critical hour, and Jesus warns that sleep and slackness leave them open to failure.
christianity.tie_back: Sleep at the decisive moment, one of the Kural’s four, is shown here as the beginning of the disciples’ collapse that night.
christianity._accuracy_note: Illustrates sleep as the road to failure; the other three vices are not named.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan puts three knots at the back of the head of any of you if he is asleep. On every knot he reads and exhales the following words, ‘The night is long, so stay asleep.’ … otherwise one gets up lazy and with a mischievous heart.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the pull of sleep as Satan whispering ‘the night is long’, which can only be broken by remembering God, washing and prayer.
islam.tie_back: ‘The night is long, so stay asleep’ is the voice of procrastination and sleep together, which is the attraction of the Kural’s pleasure boat.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on sleep, delay and resulting laziness; set in a devotional rather than worldly context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas said: morning sleep, midday wine, children’s talk and sitting in the assemblies of the ignorant put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Dosa gives a list of four comfortable habits, starting with sleeping late, that together drive a person out of the world.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the sage gives a list of four pleasant indulgences that carry a person to ruin, and oversleeping comes first.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:10 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Striking structural parallel (a list of four pleasant ruinous habits); only sleep overlaps exactly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada describes the sluggish, gluttonous person who spends his time sleeping and rolling about like a fattened hog, and says such a fool is reborn again and again.
buddhism.explanation: The verse pictures laziness and oversleeping as keeping a person trapped in the cycle of repeated birth.
buddhism.tie_back: Sleep and sloth carrying the fool around the round of rebirth is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s boat bearing the doomed to ruin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased because the page could not be re-fetched; covers sloth and sleep but not procrastination or forgetfulness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 10, Odysseus has sailed for nine days within sight of Ithaca with the bag of winds from Aeolus. He falls asleep from exhaustion, his crew open the bag, and the storm drives the ship all the way back.
greek_mythology.explanation: A single sleep at the wrong time, together with the crew’s careless curiosity, wrecks a homecoming that was almost complete.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sleep literally steers the ship to disaster, a close picture of the Kural’s ‘vessel’ of the doomed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close image match (ship plus fatal sleep); Odysseus is exhausted rather than lazy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca warns that the greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which hangs on tomorrow and loses today, and that people postpone life while it runs past them.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that habitual postponement wastes the only time we really have, the present.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s diagnosis of postponement explains the first and most dangerous passenger in the Kural’s boat, நெடுநீர்.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Brevitate Vitae 9 (trans. J. W. Basore)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on procrastination but does not address the other three vices.

kurals.tamil:
படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும் மடியுடையார்
மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Padiyudaiyaar patramaindhak kannum madiyudaiyaar
Maanpayan eydhal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: Even if the lazy come into the wealth of kings who ruled the whole earth, they will rarely get any real good out of it.
kurals.elementary: Suppose someone gives you the world’s biggest box of Lego but you never open it. You own it, but you never build anything. Having great things doesn’t help if you’re too lazy to use them.
kurals.university: படி here means ‘the earth’, so படியுடையார் are ‘those who possess the earth’, world-ruling kings. பற்று அமைதல் is ‘their possessions or support coming to one’. The classical reading (Parimelazhagar, Varadarasanar, Pappaiah) is: even if the whole wealth of such sovereigns comes to the lazy, they will rarely obtain மாண்பயன், its excellent fruit. Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read படியுடையார் as ‘worthy or powerful persons’ and பற்று as their affection or patronage: even with the favour of the great, the idle will not rise. The two readings share the same moral: fortune and connection are worthless without exertion. The couplet anticipates 610, where the tireless king gains all that Vishnu’s stride covered, and together they frame the second half of the chapter. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (கண்ணு மடியுடையார் / மாண்பய னெய்த லரிது).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Hence the king shall ever be active and discharge his duties; the root of wealth is activity, and of evil its reverse. In the absence of activity acquisitions present and to come will perish”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya concludes his chapter on royal duties by teaching that activity is the root of wealth and inactivity the root of evil: without effort, even what a king already has will perish.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Acquisitions present … will perish’ without activity is the Kural’s point that even a world-ruler’s wealth bears no fruit for the lazy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one, and also addressed to kings; the only difference is phrasing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou wicked and slothful servant … Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servant who buries his master’s money out of sloth gains nothing from it and finally loses even what he was given.
christianity.tie_back: A fortune placed in slothful hands that yields no fruit is exactly the Kural’s மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: great resources entrusted to the lazy produce nothing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that what a person gains in the end corresponds to his own striving, not to what he merely inherits or is given.
islam.tie_back: If a person gets only what he strives for, the idle heir gains nothing from a king’s wealth, which is what the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong principle match; the verse’s primary context is moral accountability before God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the lazy person, whose wishes produce nothing, with the diligent, who is richly satisfied.
judaism.tie_back: The sluggard who ‘desireth, and hath nothing’ is the Kural’s idle person for whom even great wealth yields no fruit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures fruitlessness of sloth; the proverb does not imagine the sluggard already possessing wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigālovāda Sutta, the Buddha lists six dangers of idleness: a man will not work because it is too cold, too hot, too late, too early, or because he is too hungry or too full, and so new wealth does not come to him and the wealth he has dwindles away.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha, advising a young householder, shows how the idler’s excuses stop both the gaining of new wealth and the keeping of old.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Acquired wealth dwindles’ in an idler’s hands is the same as the Kural’s claim that possessions bear no fruit for the lazy.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (trans. Nārada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in substance; paraphrased because the passage was not re-fetched.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus’ fable retold by Xenophon, Virtue tells the young Heracles at the crossroads that the gods give nothing good and fine to people without toil and effort, while Vice offers a road of ease.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles must choose between easy pleasure and hard-won goods; Virtue insists that nothing worthwhile comes without labour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Nothing good without toil’ is the positive side of the Kural’s warning that the idle get no great fruit.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a moral fable using a mythic hero rather than a myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the state of mind may exist without producing any good result, as in a man who is asleep or in some other way quite inactive, but the activity cannot … so those who act win, and rightly win, the noble and good things in life.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes possessing a good from using it: a capacity that lies unused, as in a sleeper, produces nothing, and only those who act win the prize.
philosophy.tie_back: Possession without activity producing ‘no good result’ is exactly the Kural’s lazy man holding a king’s wealth but gaining no மாண்பயன்.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8, 1098b-1099a (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Precise conceptual match (possession versus use), though Aristotle speaks of virtue, not wealth.

kurals.tamil:
இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளுஞ்சொல் கேட்பர் மடிபுரிந்து
மாண்ட உஞற்றி லவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idipurindhu ellunjol ketpar madipurindhu
Maanda unjatri lavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who give themselves to laziness and make no worthy effort will have to hear harsh rebukes and scornful words.
kurals.elementary: When you promise to help clean up and then just lie on the couch, first your friends say, ‘Come on, help!’ If you still don’t, they start to laugh at you or stop counting on you. Laziness turns friends’ nudges into teasing.
kurals.university: இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளும் சொல் combines two kinds of speech: இடி, sharp rebuke (the verb இடித்தல் is used elsewhere in the Kural for a true friend’s correction, e.g. ch. 45, 448), and எள்ளல், scornful mockery. Pappaiah and Parimelazhagar read them as a sequence: friends first rebuke the idle man, and when that fails, contempt follows. மடிபுரிந்து, ‘having embraced sloth by choice’, stresses that the laziness is willed, and the second line repeats the மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர் of 604, so this couplet adds a social consequence (loss of respect) to the material one described there. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இடிபுரிந்து as ‘slipping and falling’, a minority interpretation. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form இடிபுரிந் தெள்ளுஞ்சொற் கேட்பர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, the Kshatriya mother Vidulā finds her son Sañjaya lying dejected and inactive after a defeat, and scolds him at length, calling him a coward and urging him to rise, fight and restore his house.
hinduism.explanation: Vidulā’s rebuke of her son is a classic Indian example of a close relative using harsh words to shake someone out of inertia.
hinduism.tie_back: The idle son hearing sharp rebukes from someone close to him is exactly the இடி (rebuke) of the Kural, delivered before scorn from outsiders follows.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva 133-136 (Vidulā-putra-anuśāsana), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; Sañjaya’s inertia comes from despair after defeat as much as from sloth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed. Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.”
christianity.explanation: Speaking of members who ‘walk disorderly, working not at all’, Paul tells the church to shame the idle and admonish them as brothers.
christianity.tie_back: Brotherly admonition followed by public shame is the two-stage sequence the commentators find in இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளுஞ்சொல்.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close, including the idle-worker context of 3:11; Paul forbids treating the idler as an enemy, which softens the ‘scorn’.

islam.quote_or_event: “They were satisfied to be with those who stay behind, and their hearts were sealed over, so they do not understand.”
islam.explanation: Surat at-Tawbah reproaches the able-bodied who chose to stay at home instead of going out on the Tabuk expedition.
islam.tie_back: The Quran’s reproach of those who chose ease matches the Kural’s ‘words of rebuke’ directed at those who embrace sloth.
islam._accuracy_note: A rebuke of chosen inaction, but tied to a specific military and religious duty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.”
judaism.explanation: The father-teacher of Proverbs mocks the sluggard’s ‘little more sleep’ and warns him of the poverty that will overtake him.
judaism.tie_back: The mocking ‘How long wilt thou sleep?’ is itself an example of the rebuke and scorn the Kural says the idle must hear.
judaism._accuracy_note: Rebuke of the sluggard in direct speech; the proverb’s emphasis is on coming poverty rather than social contempt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Arise! Do not be heedless! Lead a righteous life. The righteous live happily both in this world and the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse is a direct command to wake up and stop being heedless, spoken as a teacher’s correction.
buddhism.tie_back: It reads like the ‘rebuke’ (இடி) half of the Kural: a sharp call aimed at someone who has let himself slacken.
buddhism._accuracy_note: An exhortation rather than a description of the idler’s disgrace; best available Buddhist match for this narrow point.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad Book 6, Hector finds Paris lounging in his chamber polishing his armour while the Trojans die at the walls, and rebukes him bitterly. Paris admits the rebuke is just and arms himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The prince who idles at home while others fight is shamed by his own brother, and the shame finally stirs him to act.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris hearing a brother’s just rebuke for his idleness is a dramatised version of this Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong dramatic parallel; Paris’s idleness is mixed with cowardice and sulking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius opens Book 5 of the Meditations by scolding himself for wanting to stay in bed at dawn: plants, sparrows, ants, spiders and bees all do their work, so why should a human being refuse to do his?
philosophy.explanation: The emperor turns the rebuke on himself, using the example of busy creatures to shame his own reluctance to get up and work.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus shows the Kural’s rebuke internalised: a person who would rather scold himself than hear others do it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a self-rebuke rather than reproach from others.

kurals.tamil:
மடிமை குடிமைக்கண் தங்கின்தன் ஒன்னார்க்கு
அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Madimai kudimaikkan thangindhan onnaarkku
Adimai pugutthi vidum.
kurals.meaning: If laziness settles in someone of noble birth, it will end by making him a slave to his own enemies.
kurals.elementary: A castle with strong walls is safe only while its guards stay awake. If the guards get lazy and fall asleep, the enemy walks right in. Being from a great family won’t protect you if laziness moves in.
kurals.university: The couplet depends on a rhyme chain: மடிமை (sloth), குடிமை (nobility of birth), அடிமை (slavery). The sound itself follows the slide from high birth through sloth into bondage. தங்கின், ‘if it takes up residence’, presents sloth as a lodger that gradually takes over the house. ஒன்னார், ‘those who are not one with you’, i.e. enemies, and புகுத்திவிடும், ‘will thrust one into’, give the outcome. Pope’s rendering (‘Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be’) and the Drew-Lazarus gloss both take the subject as a king of high birth, which fits the placement of the chapter in the அரசியல் (polity) section. Parimelazhagar notes that the sloth of a ruler becomes his enemies’ opportunity. The older text shows heavy sandhi (குடிமைக்கட் டங்கிற்றன் னொன்னார்க் / கடிமை) without any change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If a king is energetic, his subjects will be equally energetic. If he is reckless, they will not only be reckless likewise, but also eat into his works. Besides, a reckless king will easily fall into the hands of his enemies. Hence the king shall ever be wakeful.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya warns that a heedless king corrupts his subjects and ‘easily falls into the hands of his enemies’, so he must always stay alert.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Fall into the hands of his enemies’ is almost word for word the Kural’s ஒன்னார்க்கு அடிமை புகுத்திவிடும்.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; the Sanskrit pramatta means ‘heedless’ more than ‘lazy’, but in this context the two overlap.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that a householder who fails to keep watch lets the thief break in, using it as a picture of spiritual vigilance.
christianity.tie_back: An unwatchful master whose house is broken into is a close image of the noble whose sloth hands him to his enemies.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of loss through lack of vigilance; the teaching is eschatological, not political.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all.”
islam.explanation: Following the rebuke of those who ‘adhere heavily to the earth’ (9:38), God warns that a people who will not stir will be replaced by others.
islam.tie_back: A people displaced because they clung to ease parallels the noble house handed over to its enemies because of sloth.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on loss of position through inertia; ‘replacement’ is divine judgment, not enslavement to enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The hand of the diligent shall bear rule; But the slothful shall be under tribute.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb states a political law: the diligent end up ruling, while the lazy end up paying tribute or doing forced labour for others.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Under tribute’ (lamas, forced labour) is exactly the Kural’s அடிமை: sloth turns the free into subjects.
judaism._accuracy_note: Essentially the same maxim: sloth leads to servitude, diligence to rule.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada opens its chapter on heedfulness by teaching that heedfulness is the path to the Deathless and heedlessness the path to death: the heedful do not die, while the heedless are as if already dead.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats slack heedlessness as a condition that hands a person over to death, the ultimate enemy.
buddhism.tie_back: Heedlessness surrendering a person to death is the spiritual form of sloth surrendering the noble to his foes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the ‘enemy’ is death and craving, not political rivals, so the match is loose.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the very end of Herodotus’ Histories, Cyrus rejects a proposal that the Persians move to richer, softer lands, warning that soft lands breed soft men. The Persians agree and choose to rule a harsh land rather than sow fertile plains as slaves to others.
greek_mythology.explanation: The founding king of Persia teaches that ease and comfort turn rulers into subjects.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Slaves to others’ as the fruit of softness is the Kural’s அடிமை reached through மடிமை.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; this is Greek history with legendary colouring, not myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In chapter 14 of The Prince, Machiavelli observes that princes who have thought more of ease than of arms have lost their states, and that a prince who neglects the art of war is despised and easily undone.
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli argues that a ruler’s taste for comfort is the most common way states are lost to rivals.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli’s ease-loving prince who loses his state is Valluvar’s noble who, through sloth, becomes his enemies’ subject.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 14 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; very close in substance, though Machiavelli focuses on military neglect.

kurals.tamil:
குடியாண்மை யுள்வந்த குற்றம் ஒருவன்
மடியாண்மை மாற்றக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudiyaanmai yulvandha kutram oruvan
Madiyaanmai maatrak kedum.
kurals.meaning: When a person throws off the rule that laziness has over him, the faults that had crept into his family and his own manhood disappear.
kurals.elementary: If your room has become a mess because you kept putting things off, you don’t need magic. Start tidying today and the mess goes away. Kick out laziness and good things come back.
kurals.university: After the warnings of 601-608, the ninth couplet offers a remedy, built on the parallel compounds குடியாண்மை and மடியாண்மை. The first is read either as குடி + ஆண்மை, ‘family and manly worth’ (Varadarasanar: குடியிலும் ஆண்மையிலும்; Kalaignar: குடிப்பெருமைக்கும் ஆண்மைக்கும்), or as ‘the governing of one’s family’. The second, மடி + ஆண்மை, is ironic: sloth exercising ‘lordship’ (ஆண்மை) over a man, so that he is its subject (Pappaiah: சோம்பலுக்கு அடிமையாவது). மாற்ற, ‘when one changes, reverses’, puts the cure in the person’s own hands. Echoing 608, where sloth makes a man a slave, here overthrowing sloth’s rule restores him. The older text reads குற்ற மொருவன் with no change of sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places the responsibility for rising or falling on the individual: the same self that drags one down can lift one up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘when one changes the rule of sloth’ is the Gita’s ‘elevate yourself by yourself’ applied to laziness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on self-reform; the Gita speaks of the mind in general, not sloth or family.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.”
christianity.explanation: Paul calls on sleepers to wake and rise, promising that light will be restored to them.
christianity.tie_back: Waking from sleep so that light returns reverses the image of 601, and fits the Kural’s promise that faults vanish when sloth is overthrown.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of reversal; ‘sleep’ is spiritual deadness rather than literal idleness.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that a community’s fortune changes only when its members first change themselves inwardly.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s மாற்ற, changing one’s slothful habit so that the family’s faults disappear, is the same principle of self-change coming before restored fortune.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close structurally (inner change leads to changed condition); it does not name sloth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.”
judaism.explanation: The sluggard is told to learn from the ant, which works diligently without anyone forcing it, and to change his ways.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Consider her ways, and be wise’ is an invitation to the change of habit the Kural says will remove the family’s faults.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear call to reform sloth; the proverb does not promise the restoration of family honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who having been heedless is heedless no more, illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that someone who was once careless but has become diligent shines again, like the moon coming out from behind clouds.
buddhism.tie_back: Former heedlessness cleared away and the light returning is almost exactly the Kural’s faults vanishing when sloth is overthrown.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on reversal and restoration; family is not mentioned.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of Hercules and the Waggoner, a carter whose wagon is stuck in the mud prays to Hercules without lifting a finger. The god tells him to put his shoulder to the wheel and whip his horses, since the gods help those who help themselves.
greek_mythology.explanation: Divine help comes only after the idle man changes his behaviour and starts working himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The stuck wagon moves only when the carter stops being passive, just as the Kural says a family’s faults end when a person changes his sloth.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, Hercules and the Waggoner (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A Greek fable featuring a mythic figure; strong on self-help but has no family dimension.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Nicomachean Ethics Book II, Aristotle argues that moral virtues come about by habituation: we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so our characters are formed by the activities we repeat.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, character is not fixed; changing one’s habitual activity changes who one is.
philosophy.tie_back: Because character follows habit, Valluvar’s cure for a family’s faults is to change sloth’s ‘rule’, the habit that governs a person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, 1103a-b (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; supplies the theory behind the Kural’s remedy rather than a direct parallel.

kurals.tamil:
மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான்
தாஅய தெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Madiyilaa mannavan eydhum adiyalandhaan
Thaaaya thellaam orungu.
kurals.meaning: A king free of laziness will gain, all at once, the whole of what the God who measured the worlds with his feet strode across.
kurals.elementary: There is an old story about a god who grew so tall that he crossed the whole world in a few giant steps. This kural says a leader who is never lazy can, by working hard, win everything those giant steps covered. Hard work lets small people take giant steps too.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a Puranic allusion. அடியளந்தான், ‘he who measured with his foot’, is Vishnu as Vāmana-Trivikrama, the dwarf who asked King Mahābali for three paces of land and then grew to cover earth and heaven. தாஅயது (with அளபெடை, vowel lengthening, of தாயது, ‘what he strode across’) is therefore the whole cosmos. ஒருங்கு, ‘together, at once’, suggests that the energetic king gains all of it at once rather than piece by piece. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read it this way; Kalaignar rationalises the image into a king bringing all he traverses under his footprint. The couplet balances 606: there the idle inherit world-rulers’ wealth and gain nothing, here the tireless king gains the world. The older text has the sandhi-joined form அடியளந்தான் றாஅய தெல்லா மொருங்கு, which differs from the ytamizh reading only in how the words are split.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the dwarf Vāmana asks King Bali for three steps of land, then expands into Trivikrama, covering the earth with one stride and the heavens with the second, and leaves no room for the third.
hinduism.explanation: This is the episode the Kural alludes to: the whole of creation measured out in Vishnu’s strides, a feat already celebrated in the Rig Veda (1.154).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural promises the tireless king everything Trivikrama’s stride covered, so the myth itself is the measure of his reward.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct source of the Kural’s allusion; the myth itself is not about diligence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the pounds, the servant who worked hard with what he was given is rewarded with rule over cities.
christianity.tie_back: Diligence rewarded with wide dominion matches the Kural’s tireless king gaining the whole world.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on diligence leading to rule; the scale (ten cities versus the cosmos) differs.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed We established him upon the earth, and We gave him to everything a way.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes Dhul-Qarnayn, a righteous ruler who travels to the far west and far east and is given the means to everything.
islam.tie_back: A tireless ruler whose reach extends across the earth is the Quranic parallel to the Kural’s unsluggish king who gains all the land Vishnu strode.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel of world-spanning dominion; the verse credits God’s grant, not the ruler’s freedom from sloth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb promises that diligence raises a person to the highest company and honour.
judaism.tie_back: Diligence lifting a person to royal honour is the Kural’s point, that freedom from sloth brings the greatest possible gain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on diligence rewarded; the reward is standing before kings rather than being a world-conquering king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that the glory of one who is energetic, mindful, pure in conduct, discerning, self-controlled, righteous and heedful steadily increases.
buddhism.explanation: The verse promises ever-growing renown to the energetic and heedful person.
buddhism.tie_back: Ever-increasing glory for the energetic is the Buddhist counterpart of the Kural’s tireless king gaining everything.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased because the page could not be re-fetched; ‘glory’ is moral renown, not territorial gain.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, after completing his twelve labours and a lifetime of ceaseless toil, is taken up to Olympus at his death and made a god, receiving Hebe as his bride.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, the hero who never rested from labour is the one mortal rewarded with a place among the immortals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tireless labour earning the heavens parallels the Kural’s tireless king gaining all that a god’s stride covered.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose thematic parallel; Heracles’ reward is divinity, and his labours were imposed rather than chosen.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Way to Wealth, Franklin’s Father Abraham quotes Poor Richard that diligence is the mother of good luck and that God gives all things to industry, urging his hearers to plough deep while sluggards sleep.
philosophy.explanation: Franklin presents diligence as the source of fortune itself: what looks like luck is the reward of steady work.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘God gives all things to industry’ is almost a secular summary of the Kural’s promise to the king without sloth.
philosophy.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; close in claim (industry wins all), though addressed to ordinary people rather than kings.
